rows.notes: The study is a global literature/document review of 271 water accounts from 139 publications (Section 3 describes a systematic search of the SEEA website, WAVES, Scopus and Google Scholar; results are counts of accounts by producer, framework, scale and type). It reports no own field, survey or experimental data, so it is a review under Q1. Even if its database compilation were treated as primary, it contains no result on flow metering networks or on social cohesion: metering is never evaluated, and the only mentions relevant to the passage are generic statements that water accounts could help ensure water rights holders operate appropriately (citing the Australian Productivity Commission) and that the SEEA definition of water consumption includes apparent losses from illegal tapping. The claim that a metering network linked to a water-rights database detects illegal abstraction is not an own finding of this paper.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). The paper is a review/synthesis producing best-practice indicators (Table 4); it provides no empirical evidence on flow metering or on social outcomes.
